title: Internationalization of Graduate Education from the Periphery: A Critical Reflection from Nursing in the Brazilian Amazon
content: Internationalization has become both an organizing ideal and an evaluative metric in graduate education, yet its dominant forms remain shaped by competition, rankings, and asymmetries between academic centers and peripheries. This essay offers a conceptual and reflective contribution to that debate from an underrepresented standpoint: a graduate nursing program located in the Brazilian Amazon. Drawing on critical reflection and a purposive reading of the higher education and nursing literature, it examines how internationalization is conceptualized, how it has unfolded in Brazil, and what structural barriers and pathways shape its trajectory in regions distant from the country’s academic core. We argue that prevailing models, organized around mobility and productivity, tend to reproduce center–periphery hierarchies and to frame internationalization as an external imperative rather than a situated, relational, and ethical process. The Brazilian case shows uneven advancement, with opportunities concentrated in consolidated institutions of the South and Southeast and persistent barriers of funding instability, linguistic inequity, bureaucracy, and fragile institutional policies. Read from the Amazon, these dynamics point toward a situated internationalization grounded in equity, reciprocity, South–South cooperation, internationalization at home, and the social mission of public universities. The contribution lies in showing how a peripheral, discipline-specific standpoint can sharpen critical internationalization debates and widen the range of voices that shape the field of higher education.
